sections.title: State licensing and registration
sections.markdown: **No state license covers chimney work in Ohio.** The Ohio Construction Industry Licensing Board (OCILB, Ohio Dept. of Commerce) licenses exactly five trades under R.C. 4740.01: **heating/ventilating/air-conditioning, refrigeration, electrical, plumbing, and hydronics** contractors — masonry and general contracting are outside OCILB jurisdiction. Oversight is **municipal**: Columbus, Cleveland, and Cincinnati each run their own contractor registration/licensing programs (city sources confirmed in July pass); townships and many suburbs have nothing. "Licensed and bonded" in Ohio marketing usually means a city registration plus an insurance certificate — no exam, no state registry to check.

sections.title: What the credential does not test
sections.markdown: Bigger than anywhere: in unincorporated Ohio there may be NOTHING to verify. Individual certifications (CSIA/NCSG/NFI) and the independent audit fill a genuine vacuum — this is the strongest "why this site exists" state so far.

sections.title: Seller disclosure when a home sells
sections.markdown: **R.C. 5302.30**: Residential Property Disclosure Form required for 1–4 unit sales, delivered before the purchase contract. The official Department of Commerce form (OAC 1301:5-6-10, form eff. 6/2022) has a **Mechanical Systems section (G) whose item 6 is "Fireplace/chimney"** — the owner marks whether they know of previous or current problems or defects. Disclosure is within the seller's knowledge only; the statute says the statement "is not a substitute for any inspections" and encourages the buyer to get a professional inspection. No inspection mandate at transfer; NFPA 211 Level 2 remains standard-not-law.

sections.title: Consumer remedies and cancellation rights
sections.markdown: Ohio's strength. **Home Solicitation Sales Act (R.C. 1345.21–.28):** sales of $25 or more solicited at your home — the exact mechanics of chimney scare-sales — may be cancelled until **midnight of the third business day** after signing (R.C. 1345.22); the three-day clock does not start until the seller provides the required written agreement and cancellation notice, and until then the buyer may cancel (R.C. 1345.23). Exclusion to know: the buyer initiates contact for repair or maintenance and gives the seller a separate, dated, signed statement **in the buyer's own handwriting** describing the situation requiring immediate remedy (R.C. 1345.21; the exclusion covers only goods/services needed for that repair). **CSPA (R.C. 1345.01+) damages, R.C. 1345.09:** for an ordinary violation, rescission or actual economic damages **plus up to $5,000 in noneconomic damages**; where the act was already declared deceptive by rule or by a prior published court decision, **three times actual economic damages or $200, whichever is greater, plus up to $5,000 noneconomic damages**. The Ohio AG sues home-improvement contractors regularly; complaints via ohioattorneygeneral.gov. Door-knock "we noticed your chimney" repairs are the textbook HSSA scenario.

sections.title: Permits and building codes
sections.markdown: The **2019 Residential Code of Ohio (RCO, OAC 4101:8), based on the 2018 IRC, effective July 1, 2019**, remains the current edition. The Board of Building Standards has opened a five-year rule review of the 2019 RCO (notice July 1, 2026; stakeholder meeting July 22; draft rules filed with the CSI Office August 21; **revised rules issued September 23, 2026**, dropping the IRC electrical chapters from the proposal; **comment deadline September 30, 2026**; public hearing not yet scheduled). The BBS page does not say which IRC edition a revised RCO would rest on — a newer edition may follow; re-check before publish. Enforcement is local. Relines/rebuilds/appliance installs generally permit work; municipal variation significant (this state NEEDS the local-variance disclaimer most).

sections.title: Carbon monoxide and smoke alarm law
sections.markdown: **No Ohio Revised Code section imposing a general CO-alarm requirement on owner-occupied homes was found.** The RCO carries an IRC-style R315 for new construction (exact Ohio R315 text not reached this pass). The State Fire Marshal's Technical Bulletin TB 18-001 (Feb 2018) says the Ohio Fire Code required CO alarms in existing R occupancies with fuel-burning appliances/fireplaces or attached garages by Jan 1, 2019 — but how far the fire code reaches owner-occupied 1–2 family dwellings is not confirmed. The current Ohio Fire Code chapter 9 rule (OAC 1301:7-7-09, effective November 20, 2025) now modifies the **2021 IFC**; its section 915 text was not in the modifications document reached. Rental rules vary by city. Treat as: code-based, new construction; existing-home coverage unclear — say so on the page.

sections.title: Environmental rules and scam patterns
sections.markdown: No statewide burn regime. Ohio AG enforcement against home-improvement contractors is frequent: e.g., March 24, 2026 AG release announcing suits against four businesses including **Acme Restoration (CSPA + Home Solicitation Sales Act)**, KB Co. Builders, United Log Homes, and Atlas Exteriors; November 2025 suit against a Wood County contractor for shoddy/incomplete work. **No Ohio AG chimney-specific enforcement action found** — patterns, not names, for chimney content.

story.heading: The story
story.markdown: The triangle completes (comparison): PA registers, Michigan licenses, **Ohio does neither statewide** — its protections live in consumer law (HSSA 3-day cancel, CSPA damages, an active AG) rather than licensure. Headline: the absence, and where the leverage actually lives.
